Cavefish resist starvation by storing fat and live healthily with high blood sugar and insulin resistance
Compensates for blindness with more taste buds and an enhanced lateral line

animal.diet: Omnivore: insects, small crustaceans, algae and detritus; cavefish eat bat guano and organic debris
animal.habitat: Surface: clear streams and rivers; cave forms: pools and streams of limestone caves
animal.lifespan: Up to about 15 years in captivity
animal.size: Up to about 12 cm
animal.behaviour: Surface fish school by day, while cave fish forage alone along the bottom with their heads tilted down.
fieldMarks: Surface form: silvery tetra with a dark spot or stripe at the tail base and reddish fins
Cave form: pink-white, no visible eyes, skin over the eye sockets
Adipose fin present in both
animal.lookalikes: Other Astyanax tetras in Central America (A. aeneus and others) are only told apart in the hand. In the caves of the Sierra de El Abra region, no other eyeless fish looks like it.
animal.whereToSee: Cueva de El Pachón and Sótano de la Tinaja (permits needed); surface fish in the Río Tampaón and Río Guayalejo; aquaria and research labs
animal.season: Resident; cavefish breed opportunistically year-round

lore: Mexican biologist Salvador Coronado collected the first blind cavefish at the Cueva Chica in 1936, and they were described as a new genus, Anoptichthys, before they were found to interbreed with river tetras. Darwin, writing before this discovery, had argued that cave animals lose their eyes through disuse.
funFact: Blind cavefish and sighted surface fish can still interbreed, and some of the hybrids have partial eyes.

summary: A tiny, live-bearing fish of Trinidad and northern South America whose wildly patterned males made it a star of evolution research and the world's best-known aquarium fish. It has been released worldwide to eat mosquito larvae.
nativeRange: North-eastern South America (Venezuela, Guyana, Suriname, northern Brazil) and Trinidad, Tobago and Barbados; introduced across the tropics
abilities: Gives birth to live young; females store sperm and can have several broods from one mating
Wild populations evolve duller or brighter males within a few generations depending on predators, as shown by experiments in Trinidad
Tolerates polluted, warm and brackish water

animal.diet: Omnivore: algae, mosquito and other insect larvae, small invertebrates and detritus
animal.habitat: Shallow streams, pools, ditches and ponds, including disturbed and polluted waters
animal.size: Males about 2–3 cm; females to about 5 cm
animal.behaviour: Males constantly court females with sigmoid displays or attempt sneaky matings. Females prefer males with more orange.
fieldMarks: Males tiny with mosaic patterns of orange, black, blue and iridescent spots, and often a large tail
Females larger, drab olive-grey, with a dark 'gravid spot' near the vent
Male anal fin modified into a tube-like gonopodium
Upturned mouth
animal.lookalikes: Mosquitofish (Gambusia) are similar livebearers but males are plain grey, sometimes with black spots. Endler's guppy (Poecilia wingei) from Venezuela has smaller, more metallic males.
animal.whereToSee: Streams of Trinidad's Northern Range (Aripo and Yarra rivers); drains and canals across the tropics where introduced
animal.season: Resident; breeds year-round

lore: Named after Robert John Lechmere Guppy, who sent specimens from Trinidad to the British Museum in 1866. John Endler's experiments in Trinidad in the late 1970s, moving guppies above waterfalls, became a classic demonstration of natural selection in the wild.
funFact: Female guppies can store sperm for months, so a single female introduced to new water can found a whole population.

otherNames: Pla kat ปลากัด (Thai)
summary: A small air-breathing fish of Thai paddies and marshes, bred over centuries for combat and later for flowing colourful fins. Wild populations are now Vulnerable as their wetlands vanish.
nativeRange: Central Thailand and the Chao Phraya and Mekong basins (Cambodia, Laos, Vietnam); introduced elsewhere
abilities: Breathes air with a labyrinth organ, so it survives in tiny, stagnant puddles
Males build floating bubble nests and guard eggs and fry
Males flare their gill covers and fins in aggressive displays to rivals

animal.diet: Carnivore: insects and their larvae, zooplankton
animal.habitat: Shallow, still, vegetated waters: paddies, marshes and floodplain pools
animal.lifespan: About 2–3 years; up to 5 in captivity
animal.size: Around 6 cm
animal.behaviour: Males guard a territory and a bubble nest. After spawning they catch falling eggs in their mouths and place them in the nest.
fieldMarks: Wild males: dull reddish-brown with iridescent blue-green scales and red-tinted fins
Domestic males: very long, flowing fins in reds, blues and whites
Upturned mouth; long anal fin and short dorsal set back
Females smaller and duller, with shorter fins
animal.lookalikes: Other wild Betta species (B. imbellis, B. smaragdina, B. mahachaiensis) are very similar and best told apart by range and fin and colour details. Gouramis have thread-like pelvic fins.
animal.whereToSee: Paddy fields and marshes of central Thailand (wild fish increasingly rare); fish markets of Bangkok's Chatuchak; aquaria worldwide
animal.season: Resident; breeds in the rainy season (May–October)

lore: Siamese villagers bred short-finned fighting strains (pla kat) for wagering for centuries, and King Rama III is said to have licensed and taxed the fights. In 2019 Thailand declared the betta its national aquatic animal.
funFact: The genus name Betta may come from the Malay 'ikan bettah', and splendens means 'splendid'.

summary: A small striped minnow of South Asian paddies and streams that became one of biology's most important laboratory animals. Its transparent embryos develop in days, and it can regrow its heart, fins and retina.
nativeRange: India, Bangladesh, Nepal and Bhutan (Ganges and Brahmaputra basins), possibly Pakistan and Myanmar
abilities: Regrows damaged heart muscle, fins, spinal cord and retina
Embryos are transparent and develop from egg to swimming larva in about 3 days
About 70% of human genes have a zebrafish counterpart, making it a model for disease research

animal.diet: Omnivore: zooplankton, insects and larvae, algae
animal.habitat: Shallow, still or slow-flowing vegetated water, including rice paddies
animal.size: Up to about 4 cm
animal.behaviour: Forms shoals and spawns at dawn, with females scattering eggs over vegetation and gravel.
fieldMarks: Slender, small minnow body with 5–7 horizontal blue-black stripes running to the tail tip
Silvery-gold to yellow stripes between the dark ones
Two pairs of barbels
Striped anal fin
animal.lookalikes: Pearl danio (Devario/Danio albolineatus) has no stripes but a pinkish iridescent sheen. Giant danio (Devario aequipinnatus) is bigger, with broken stripes and a yellow ground colour.
animal.whereToSee: Paddy fields and streams of West Bengal and Bangladesh during the monsoon; research labs worldwide
animal.season: Resident; breeds mostly in the monsoon

lore: Buchanan-Hamilton described it from the Ganges in 1822. George Streisinger at the University of Oregon developed it as a lab model in the 1970s, and his 1981 Nature paper on producing clonal, homozygous zebrafish launched zebrafish genetics.
funFact: The zebrafish's stripes self-organise through interactions between three kinds of pigment cells, a textbook living example of the pattern-forming mechanism proposed by Alan Turing.

otherNames: Pla sua phon nam ปลาเสือพ่นน้ำ (Thai)
summary: A mangrove fish that shoots down insects with a jet of water fired from its mouth, correcting for the bending of light at the surface. Experiments show it can learn to recognise human faces.
nativeRange: Coasts and estuaries from India and Sri Lanka through Southeast Asia to northern Australia, New Guinea and the western Pacific islands
abilities: Spits jets of water up to about 2 m, pressing its tongue against a groove in the roof of its mouth to form a barrel
Shapes the jet so the water's tail catches up with its head and lands as a heavier blob
Corrects for light refraction at the water surface when aiming
Can learn to tell a familiar human face from dozens of others

animal.diet: Carnivore: insects and spiders shot from overhanging leaves; also crustaceans and small fish in the water
animal.habitat: Brackish mangrove creeks and estuaries; sometimes coastal reefs and freshwater streams
animal.lifespan: Up to around 10 years in captivity
animal.size: Usually 10–20 cm; up to 30 cm
animal.behaviour: It cruises near the surface, often in small groups, and leaps to snatch prey within reach. Group members race to the fallen prey, so shooters predict where it will land.
fieldMarks: Deep, compressed silvery-white body with a flat back from snout to dorsal fin
Four or five bold, black, wedge-shaped bars along the upper side
Large eyes and a sharply upturned mouth
Dorsal fin set far back above the anal fin
animal.lookalikes: Seven-spot archerfish (T. chatareus) has more numerous, smaller black spots and lives more often in fresh water. Spotted scat (Scatophagus argus) is rounder, with many dark spots and no flat back.
animal.whereToSee: Mangroves of the Sundarbans; Kinabatangan River (Sabah); Kakadu (Australia); public aquaria
animal.season: Resident year-round

lore: Western naturalists heard reports of the shooting fish from the Dutch East Indies in the 1760s. The genus name Toxotes means 'archer' and jaculatrix 'thrower of darts'.
funFact: In 2016 Oxford researchers trained archerfish to spit at one human face out of 44, which they did with over 80% accuracy.

otherNames: Pla kapong khao ปลากะพงขาว (Thai)
summary: A large silver predator of Indo-Pacific rivers, estuaries and coasts that migrates downriver to spawn at sea. All barramundi are born male and most later change sex to female. In Bengal it is bhetki, the fish of the classic fish fry.
nativeRange: Persian Gulf and Arabian Sea coasts east through South Asia and Southeast Asia to southern China, Taiwan, Papua New Guinea and northern Australia
abilities: Catadromous: grows in rivers and swims to estuaries and coastal seas to spawn
Protandrous hermaphrodite: born male, it usually becomes female at about 3–5 years old and 80–100 cm
Lives in fresh, brackish or salt water
A big female can release tens of millions of eggs in a season
edibilityNote: Firm, mild white fillets; widely farmed. Bengal's bhetki fish fry and paturi are classics. Always cooked. Large wild fish from polluted estuaries may carry mercury.

animal.diet: Carnivore: fish, prawns, crabs and insects
animal.habitat: Rivers, billabongs, mangrove estuaries and coastal waters
animal.size: Commonly 60–120 cm; up to about 2 m and 60 kg
animal.behaviour: Adults move down to river mouths and coastal flats at the start of the wet season to spawn on spring tides. Juveniles move up into freshwater swamps and creeks to grow.
fieldMarks: Silver body with a concave forehead and a pointed head
Large mouth with the jaw extending behind the eye; red-glowing eye at night
Spiny and soft dorsal fins almost separate; rounded tail
Freshwater fish golden-bronze; estuarine and sea fish silver
animal.lookalikes: Nile perch (L. niloticus) occurs only in Africa. Mangrove jack (Lutjanus argentimaculatus) has a reddish tint and canine teeth. Giant perch (Lates japonicus) of Japan is very similar.
animal.whereToSee: Kakadu and the Northern Territory rivers (Australia); the Sundarbans and Hooghly estuary; Thai fish markets
animal.season: Spawning migrations to estuaries at the start of the wet season (October–February in northern Australia; monsoon in South Asia)

lore: The name barramundi comes from an Aboriginal language of central Queensland and was popularised as a market name in Australia from the 1980s. Rock art in Kakadu and Arnhem Land includes 'X-ray' paintings of barramundi showing their spine and organs.
funFact: Because they change sex as they grow, almost all the very large barramundi are females.

summary: The largest of the sturgeons and one of the biggest bony fish ever recorded, a long-lived giant of the Caspian and Black Seas that runs up the Volga, Ural and Danube to spawn. Poaching for beluga caviar has driven it to Critically Endangered.
nativeRange: Caspian and Black Sea basins (formerly also the Adriatic and Sea of Azov), with spawning runs up the Volga, Ural, Kura, Danube and other large rivers
abilities: Lives over 100 years and may not first spawn until about 15–20 years old
Anadromous: migrates from the sea hundreds of kilometres up large rivers to spawn on gravel beds
Hunts fish with a huge crescent-shaped mouth, unlike the bottom-sucking smaller sturgeons
Historic females weighed over 1,000 kg, a quarter of it roe
edibilityNote: Beluga caviar is the most expensive caviar. International trade in wild beluga caviar is effectively closed under CITES, and buying it supports poaching, so choose certified farmed caviar only. Long-lived sturgeon accumulate mercury and other contaminants. Raw sturgeon flesh should be avoided.

animal.diet: Carnivore: fish (gobies, herring, carp, other sturgeon), crustaceans and molluscs; occasionally seals
animal.habitat: Open waters of the Caspian and Black Seas; large rivers during spawning
animal.size: Commonly 2–3 m and 100–300 kg; historically up to about 6–7 m and 1,500 kg
animal.behaviour: Spring and autumn runs move upriver, and autumn migrants overwinter in deep river pits before spawning the following spring.
fieldMarks: Huge, crescent-shaped mouth stretching nearly across the underside of the head
Short, pointed snout; flattened, leaf-shaped barbels
Five rows of bony scutes (back, sides and belly); dark grey above, pale below
Shark-like tail with a longer upper lobe
animal.lookalikes: Russian sturgeon (Acipenser gueldenstaedtii) and stellate sturgeon (A. stellatus) have much smaller mouths and round barbels, and the stellate sturgeon has a very long, narrow snout. The kaluga (Huso dauricus) of the Amur basin is its only true relative.
animal.whereToSee: The Volga delta near Astrakhan; the lower Danube at the Iron Gates (where dams block the old runs); hatcheries and aquaria
animal.season: Upriver spawning runs in spring (March–May) and autumn (August–November)

lore: Herodotus described the great boneless fish of the Borysthenes (Dnieper), called antacaei, that the Scythians salted. Russian tsars and Persian shahs drew huge revenues from Caspian caviar, and a beluga of about 1,571 kg was reported from the Volga estuary in 1827.
funFact: Isinglass, a gelatin once used to clarify beer and wine, was first made from the dried swim bladders of sturgeons such as the beluga.

summary: A big, shark-like filter feeder of the Mississippi basin with a long, flat paddle for a snout. The paddle is covered in electroreceptors that detect swarms of plankton. Its only recent relative, the Chinese paddlefish, was declared extinct in 2022.
nativeRange: Mississippi River basin and nearby Gulf Coast drainages of the United States; extirpated from Canada and the Great Lakes
abilities: Its paddle-shaped rostrum carries tens of thousands of electroreceptors that sense the weak electric fields of zooplankton
Swims with its mouth agape, sieving plankton through comb-like gill rakers
Makes long upstream spawning migrations, sometimes hundreds of kilometres
Belongs to a lineage that goes back over 100 million years; very similar fossils occur in Montana
edibilityNote: Firm white flesh; the roe is sold as American caviar and is a major target of poaching. Commercial and sport harvest is limited to strict seasons. Long-lived fish can accumulate mercury, PCBs and chlordane in some rivers, so follow local advisories.

animal.diet: Filter-feeder: zooplankton (water fleas, copepods) and insect larvae
animal.habitat: Slow, deep, open water of large rivers, oxbows and reservoirs
animal.size: Commonly 1–1.5 m; up to about 2.2 m and 90 kg
animal.behaviour: In spring, adults migrate upriver during floods to spawn over gravel bars. The sticky eggs hatch within days and the larvae drift downstream.
fieldMarks: Long, flat, paddle-shaped snout (about a third of body length in adults)
Smooth, scaleless grey to bluish skin
Huge mouth and a long, pointed, flap-like gill cover
Shark-like tail with a longer upper lobe
animal.lookalikes: Shovelnose sturgeon (Scaphirhynchus platorynchus) has bony scutes, a shovel-shaped snout and barbels in front of a small mouth on the underside. No other fish in its range has a long paddle snout.
animal.whereToSee: Osage River and Lake of the Ozarks (Missouri); Grand Lake o' the Cherokees (Oklahoma); Gavins Point Dam on the Missouri (South Dakota/Nebraska) during spring snagging season
animal.season: Spawning migrations March–May when rivers rise; snagging seasons in spring

lore: Native peoples of the Mississippi basin fished paddlefish long before European contact. Johann Walbaum described it in 1792 as a kind of shark, Squalus spathula.
funFact: Paddlefish with their paddle removed can still feed normally, because electroreceptors on the head and gill covers take over, but the paddle greatly extends their detection range.

summary: A giant armoured fish of southern US rivers and bayous with a broad, alligator-like snout and a double row of fangs. It belongs to a lineage that has changed little for about 100 million years, and its eggs are poisonous.
nativeRange: Lower Mississippi basin and Gulf of Mexico coastal drainages from Florida to Veracruz, Mexico
abilities: Breathes air with a vascularised swim bladder, so it survives warm, stagnant backwaters
Its interlocking diamond-shaped ganoid scales form armour that resists most predators
Lies motionless like a log, then sideswipes fish with its toothed snout
Lives for many decades: fish over 50 years old have been aged from their ear stones (otoliths), and ages near 95 have been reported
edibilityNote: The white flesh is eaten in the US South and Mexico (gar balls, fried gar). The eggs are toxic: gar roe contains an ichthyotoxin that causes vomiting, diarrhoea and other illness in humans, and must never be eaten. The skin and scales are extremely hard to cut, and large old fish may carry mercury.

animal.diet: Carnivore: fish, crabs, turtles and water birds; scavenges carcasses
animal.habitat: Slow, large rivers, oxbow lakes, bayous, reservoirs and brackish bays
animal.size: Commonly 1.5–2 m; up to about 3 m and 150 kg
animal.behaviour: Floats near the surface and rolls to gulp air. In spring, groups spawn over flooded vegetation, scattering sticky green eggs that hatch within days.
fieldMarks: Broad, short, alligator-like snout
Two rows of large teeth in the upper jaw on each side (other gars have one)
Long, torpedo-shaped body armoured with diamond-shaped ganoid scales
Dorsal and anal fins set far back near the rounded tail; olive-brown above
animal.lookalikes: Longnose gar (Lepisosteus osseus) has a very long, needle-thin beak. Spotted and shortnose gars are smaller (under 1 m), with narrower snouts and a single row of large upper teeth. Florida gar has spots all over.
animal.whereToSee: The Trinity River (Texas); Louisiana bayous and the Atchafalaya Basin; the lower Mississippi and its oxbow lakes
animal.season: Resident; spawns April–June when floods inundate vegetation

lore: Native peoples of the lower Mississippi used gar scales as arrowheads and the skin as armour. Early settlers covered wooden ploughshares with gar hide. In the 20th century gars were persecuted as 'trash fish' until research showed their role in river ecosystems.
funFact: Gar roe is toxic to mammals and birds, which may help protect the eggs from egg-eating predators.

summary: A living fossil from the age of dinosaurs and one of only two surviving species in an order otherwise known from Jurassic and Cretaceous fossils. It can gulp air and lie up in swamp mud, and fathers guard their young fiercely.
nativeRange: Atlantic and Gulf coastal plain of the south-eastern United States (since 2022 the northern and inland bowfins are a separate species, A. ocellicauda)
abilities: Breathes air through a lung-like swim bladder, so it survives warm, stagnant swamps
Can survive in burrows in drying mud
Males clear nests, then herd and guard a black ball of fry for weeks
Its order, Amiiformes, dates back to the Jurassic
edibilityNote: Eaten in Louisiana as choupique, often fried, smoked or made into fishcakes; the roe is sold as 'Cajun caviar'. The flesh is soft and is best cooked fresh. Unlike gar, bowfin eggs are not toxic.

animal.diet: Carnivore: fish, crayfish, frogs, insects and other prey
animal.habitat: Swamps, bayous, sloughs and weedy, slow waters
animal.size: Commonly 45–60 cm; up to about 1.1 m
animal.behaviour: Hunts at night among weeds. In spring the male builds a circular nest in vegetation, attracts females, and then guards eggs and the swarm of fry.
fieldMarks: Long, cylindrical body with a very long, wavy dorsal fin running along most of the back
Bony gular plate between the lower jaws
Black eyespot at the upper tail base, ringed in orange in males
Short anal fin; rounded tail; tubular nostrils
Breeding males with bright green fins and belly
animal.lookalikes: Eyetail bowfin (Amia ocellicauda) is almost identical and is separated mainly by range and genetics. Northern snakehead (Channa argus, introduced) has a long anal fin, no gular plate and a scaled head. Burbot has a chin barbel and two dorsal fins.
animal.whereToSee: Okefenokee Swamp (Georgia); Florida's St. Johns River; blackwater rivers of the Carolina and Georgia coastal plain
animal.season: Resident; spawns in spring (March–May in the south)

lore: In Louisiana, bowfins have been sold as choupique (from a Choctaw word) as a cheap food fish for generations. When the Caspian caviar trade collapsed, bowfin roe became a domestic caviar substitute.
funFact: The bowfin's order has fossils on several continents, but today only the two North American bowfin species survive.

summary: A living link to the fish that first crawled onto land, almost unchanged from fossils about 100 million years old. Unlike other lungfishes it breathes mostly with gills, using its single lung in low-oxygen water.
nativeRange: South-eastern Queensland, Australia: Burnett and Mary rivers (native); translocated to the Brisbane, Albert, Pine and Coomera rivers
abilities: Breathes with gills and a single lung, gulping air when water is warm or oxygen-poor
Has one of the largest animal genomes ever sequenced, at about 43 billion base pairs
Lives for many decades; one in captivity lived over 90 years
Detects prey with electroreceptors on the snout

animal.diet: Omnivore: snails, worms, shrimps, frogs, small fish and plants
animal.habitat: Slow-flowing, deep pools of rivers with aquatic plants and soft beds
animal.size: Up to about 1.5 m and 40 kg
animal.behaviour: Moves slowly along the bottom using its flipper-like fins. It lays eggs singly among water plants in spring, and the eggs rely on the plant beds that dams and weirs destroy.
fieldMarks: Heavy, elongate body covered in very large, overlapping scales
Paddle-shaped, fleshy pectoral and pelvic fins on stalk-like bases
Continuous fin around the rear body forming a pointed tail
Olive-brown to grey above, often with dark spots; pale belly
animal.lookalikes: Introduced and native catfishes have barbels and no large scales. African and South American lungfishes look different and do not occur in Australia: they are eel-like, with threadlike fins and small scales.
animal.whereToSee: Mary River and Burnett River (Queensland); Wivenhoe and Somerset dams; Queensland Museum and public aquaria
animal.season: Resident; spawns August–December

lore: Gerard Krefft described it in 1870 from a fish sent to him by William Forster, a Queensland squatter. The Mary River Traveston Crossing Dam was cancelled in 2009 under Australian environmental law, partly because of its threat to lungfish.
funFact: 'Granddad', an Australian lungfish at Chicago's Shedd Aquarium from 1933 to 2017, was the oldest aquarium fish on record when he died.

summary: An eel-like air-breather of West African floodplains that survives the dry season sealed in a mucus cocoon in baked mud for months, sometimes years. It walks along the bottom on thin, thread-like fins, a hint of how the first vertebrates moved onto land.
nativeRange: West and Central Africa: from Senegal and Gambia through the Niger, Volta and Lake Chad basins, with populations also in parts of the Congo basin
abilities: Aestivates: it burrows into mud, secretes a mucus cocoon that hardens, and breathes air through a tube to the surface while its metabolism slows
Obligate air-breather that drowns if kept from the surface
Walks and bounds along the bottom with its slender pelvic fins, a gait studied as a model for the origin of tetrapod walking
Males guard the nest and aerate the eggs
edibilityNote: Eaten in West Africa, often dug out of dry-season mud. Always cooked. As a bottom dweller in floodplains it can carry parasites and accumulate contaminants.

animal.diet: Omnivore: snails, crustaceans, insect larvae, fish, frogs and plant matter
animal.habitat: Seasonal swamps, floodplains, marshes and river margins that may dry out
animal.size: Usually 50–70 cm; up to about 1 m
animal.behaviour: As waters recede it wriggles into the mud and curls up in a cocoon, and it emerges when the rains return. Males dig nests and guard eggs and larvae.
fieldMarks: Eel-like body with a continuous fin around the rear
Long, thin, thread-like pectoral and pelvic fins with a fringe on the pectorals
Olive-brown to grey with dark spots, pale belly
Small eyes and a short, rounded snout
animal.lookalikes: Marbled lungfish (Protopterus aethiopicus) of East Africa is larger, with marbled patterning. True eels and spiny eels have no thread-like paired fins.
animal.whereToSee: Gambia River floodplains; the Inner Niger Delta (Mali); rice-growing wetlands of Senegal and Guinea-Bissau
animal.season: Active in the rainy season (roughly June–October); aestivates in the dry season

lore: Richard Owen described it in 1839 as Lepidosiren annectens, 'the connecting one', because it seemed to link fish and amphibians. Lungfish cocoons dug from Gambian mud were shipped alive to Europe, where they 'woke' in aquaria.
funFact: In 2011 researchers filmed this species lifting its body and walking on its pelvic fins along the bottom, a gait once thought to have arisen only in tetrapods.
